questions: Is this walking pattern new or noticeably worse than your usual walking?
Did it begin suddenly, over hours or days?
Have you ever had a stroke or transient ischemic attack?
Do you currently have weakness on one side of your body?
Does one leg frequently drag, buckle, or give way?
Do you have numbness or reduced sensation in either leg or your feet?
Do you have difficulty feeling where your feet are when your eyes are closed?
Do you feel dizzy, off-balance, or as if the room is spinning?
Do you have double vision, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, or new difficulty coordinating your hands?
Have you recently developed a severe or unusual headache?
Do you have tremor, especially when your hands or legs are at rest?
Do you feel unusually stiff or slowed in your movements?
Do you take unusually small steps or have difficulty initiating walking or turning?
Have you had falls or near-falls recently?
Do you have pain in your hips, knees, ankles, or feet when walking?
Does one leg feel shorter, rotated, or difficult to place normally?
Do you have back pain radiating into either leg?
Have you lost control of your bladder or bowels?
Do you have numbness around your groin or inner thighs?
Have you had fever, recent infection, or a recent injury?
Have you started or changed any medications or used alcohol or recreational drugs before this walking problem began?
Do you have diabetes, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, a known nerve disorder, or another neurological condition?
Has a clinician previously told you that you have a problem with your balance or walking?
Is someone assisting you or using a wheelchair because you cannot walk safely without help?

results: 1. Focused bedside neurological examination, including eye movements, nystagmus, dysarthria, limb coordination, truncal stability, and gait
coordination examination (limb and truncal): limb and truncal ataxia
3. Noncontrast CT scan of the head
4. CT angiography of the head and neck
5. MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted and susceptibility-weighted sequences
brain MRI: cerebellar atrophy at one year; serial imaging over five years shows progressive ISOLATED cerebellar atrophy with no supratentorial abnormality
6. Complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, liver function, calcium, magnesium, and serum glucose
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
serum calcium, magnesium and phosphate: normal
8. Prothrombin time/INR and activated partial thromboplastin time
9. Serum ethanol level and urine toxicology screen
10. Serum concentrations of any potentially neurotoxic or sedating medication recently started or dose-increased
serum lithium and drug levels: serum lithium 4.07 mmol/L on admission; CSF lithium 2.45 mmol/L; later fell below 0.2 mmol/L
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Lithium-induced cerebellar neurotoxicity causing progressive cerebellar degeneration and ataxia (SILENT syndrome—syndrome of irreversible lithium-effectuated neurotoxicity)

ALTERNATIVE: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration

ALTERNATIVE: Hereditary spinocerebellar ataxia

ALTERNATIVE: Autoimmune cerebellar ataxia
